name: open-host-service
intent: Give a subsystem that many callers depend on one documented, versioned protocol they all integrate through, so the upstream owns a single stable contract instead of a translator per consumer and its internal model stays private.
problem: A subsystem in high demand is dragged into per-consumer integration work: every new caller either couples to the internal model - so each internal change risks breaking a consumer - or asks the upstream team for another bespoke translator, and the integration surface grows with the number of consumers instead of staying constant.
context: Strategic design at a subsystem boundary where one bounded context, service, platform or library is upstream of several independent consumers that do not share its model or its release cadence. It applies when the upstream controls its own interface and is willing to own documentation, versioning and deprecation; typically microservice platforms, shared internal platforms, partner-facing APIs and legacy subsystems that must be opened up.
benefits: One integration surface instead of N: new consumers integrate against the published protocol without the upstream team writing another bespoke translator.
Internal models stay private: the protocol representation (DTOs, messages, schema) is a deliberate subset, so domain refactorings no longer ripple into every consumer.
Release cadences decouple: consumers migrate on their own schedule, and a versioning policy with a deprecation window replaces coordinated big-bang upgrades.

The contract becomes a machine-readable artifact (OpenAPI document, .proto, GraphQL SDL, versioned ABI), so client generation, mock servers, contract tests and documentation all derive from one source.
Boundary concerns are centralised: authentication, authorisation, rate limiting, quotas and audit live at the single published entry point instead of being re-solved per consumer.
Idiosyncratic consumers can be served by one-off translators in front of the shared protocol, keeping the protocol itself simple and coherent.
tradeoffs: The protocol outlives the internal model: every future domain change must be re-expressed in protocol terms and old shapes kept working until consumers migrate, so the upstream acquires a permanent compatibility, deprecation and documentation obligation.

A second model must be maintained next to the domain model - the wire DTOs/schema plus the mapper - and kept in sync with the code; drift between a generated document and a hand-written spec is the classic failure mode.

Designing for many clients pulls the contract toward the lowest common denominator: either a generic CRUD surface that loses the domain's expressiveness, or a contract bloated with every consumer's special cases; Evans' remedy - serve idiosyncratic needs with one-off translators - only works if that scope creep is refused.
A published surface is a public attack surface and a public performance profile: the wire format, authentication scheme and rate limits become long-lived public decisions made under load.

Stability removes the feedback pressure that per-consumer translators created: without a named owner and consumer-side contract tests, the protocol rots - reachable, documented once, and slowly wrong.
The pattern creates a protocol-owner role (schema, docs, versioning policy, migration support) that has to be funded; nothing in the pattern produces that role by itself.

participants.responsibility: Owns the subsystem and decides which capabilities become published services; remains the only writer of the protocol.
The stable, documented contract consumers bind to: operations/messages, their data shapes (often carried by a Published Language) and the versioning policy for evolving them.
Maps internal model to protocol representation and back; the only component that knows both, so neither model leaks into the other.
Keeps the contract documented, versioned and deprecation-managed: schema artifact, changelog, migration notes, usage tracking, contract tests.
Integrates exclusively through the protocol; may conform to it as-is or wrap it in its own anticorruption layer, but never reads upstream internals.
Augments the shared protocol for a single consumer's idiosyncratic needs so the published protocol stays simple and coherent.

use_cases: A platform service consumed by many product teams (billing, identity, notifications, document generation) that otherwise fields a steady stream of one-off integration requests.
Opening a legacy subsystem to new consumers: its old model is mapped once to a published protocol instead of being copied into each new client.

A library or SDK with many downstream code bases: a documented public API plus an explicit versioning policy - and, in ABI-sensitive languages, versioned symbols - is the same pattern for in-process consumers.
Microservice context maps where one upstream context serves several downstream contexts, some of them conformist and some carrying their own anticorruption layer.
A partner-facing API where third parties integrate through the documented, authenticated protocol while internal models, tooling and deployment details stay hidden.

Kubernetes' API server is the common REST boundary for control-plane components and external commands; its alpha, beta and stable API versions make lifecycle and migration explicit while clients remain independent of the server's implementation.

Stripe's partner-facing API pins an account or request to a documented API version, separates backward-compatible monthly releases from breaking major releases, and versions webhook payloads so independent integrations can migrate deliberately.

GitHub's REST API exposes one documented service to many clients through date-named versions and the X-GitHub-Api-Version header; additive changes are shared while breaking changes receive a new version and a migration window.
avoid_when: Only one or two known consumers: a direct contract negotiated with those teams, plus their own anticorruption layer, is cheaper than building and governing a public protocol.
The upstream model is already acceptable and stable to its consumers: a conformist relationship avoids the second model and the versioning policy entirely.
Each consumer can and should own the translation (downstream wraps the upstream in an anticorruption layer): publishing a protocol only helps if the upstream is willing to own it.
The parts have no significant relationship at all: declare separate ways rather than inventing a protocol to share.
An API gateway or integration layer already publishes the surface for you (routing, versioning, documentation, authentication): do not build a second publication mechanism behind it.
anti_patterns: A protocol that grows one endpoint per consumer until it is every consumer's special case - the shared surface becomes the maintenance burden the pattern was meant to remove.
Publishing the internal model as the protocol: once the domain model is the interchange language it is effectively frozen and can no longer respond to internal development.
Big-bang version changes - an incompatible v2 with no migration path, deprecation window or contract tests - presented as 'a new version'.
A so-called published protocol that is neither documented nor owned: consumers reverse-engineer it from observed behaviour and every change silently breaks someone.
Per-consumer authentication and payload validation performed downstream instead of at the host boundary, forcing every consumer to re-implement the same checks.
design_principles: Information hiding: only the protocol representation crosses the boundary; the domain model, its invariants and its persistence stay internal.
Stable interface: the protocol is an explicit artifact under version control (IDL, schema document, versioned headers/symbols), not a by-product of the current code.
Dependency inversion: consumers depend on the published protocol, never on the host's types, modules or database.
Open/closed at the protocol level: extend by adding capabilities and optional fields; existing consumers keep binding to the shapes they already know.
Single responsibility: one owner for the protocol, its documentation, versioning policy and deprecation process.
Translate at the seam: exactly one layer knows both models (facade/mapper), so neither side leaks into the other.
best_practices: Publish the contract as a versioned artifact (OpenAPI document, .proto, GraphQL SDL, versioned ABI) and generate clients, mocks and documentation from it.
Keep DTOs distinct from domain types and translate explicitly at the boundary; never serialise aggregates or persistence entities.
Decide the versioning policy before the first consumer integrates (path, media type, header, or additive-only schema evolution) and write the deprecation window down.
Allow only additive changes inside a version; a breaking change creates a new version whose predecessor stays served until consumers have migrated.
Test the protocol from the consumer's side - contract tests, example payloads, generated SDKs - and version the document together with the code.
Keep one owner for the protocol and a public changelog; mark deprecated fields explicitly and measure their usage before removing them.
Serve idiosyncratic consumers with one-off translators in front of the published protocol instead of extending the protocol for them.
sources: Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software (2003) - Context Mapping chapter: Open Host Service, Published Language, Anticorruption Layer, Conformist.
Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design Reference: Definitions and Pattern Summaries (2015) - Open Host Service (p. 35) and Published Language (p. 36).
